output_text: We reanalysed the ChEMBL nintedanib activity table (CHEMBL502835; 2,250 records) for PDGFRA (CHEMBL2007; UniProt P16234) and FLT4 (CHEMBL1955; UniProt P35916). The specified exact-relation, human, validity-clean, nonduplicate record set restricted to the BioAssay Ontology label “single protein format” remained the primary analysis. IC50, Kd and Ki were analysed separately. We reported individual deposited values, assay and source-document counts, medians and observed ranges, without treating heterogeneous literature assays as biological replicates or pooling IC50 with affinity constants. Document-balanced summaries used the median pChEMBL within each endpoint–document stratum, followed by the median across documents. Leave-one-document-out analyses assessed sensitivity to individual sources. Comparisons between targets were restricted to the same source document and endpoint and were descriptive because assay conditions could still differ. A labelled sensitivity analysis relaxed only the BioAssay Ontology format restriction while retaining human target identity, exact relation, available pChEMBL, absence of validity warnings and absence of duplicate flags. This sensitivity analysis did not update the fixed integrated ranking. Every target-specific raw record received an auditable disposition; missing kinetic values were not imputed.

Assay-stratified review retained seven PDGFRA measurements from seven assays and seven source documents and four FLT4 measurements from four assays and four documents. The primary IC50 medians were 18 nM for PDGFRA (five measurements; range 1.9–560 nM) and 13 nM for FLT4 (three measurements; range 5–34 nM; Fig. 4A,B). Separate equilibrium-binding records reported Kd values of 16 nM and 95 nM, respectively, and one PDGFRA inhibition-constant record reported Ki=8.4 nM. These measurements provide an experimental pharmacological basis for evaluating both receptors, while the 560-nM PDGFRA record shows that apparent potency varies substantially across assay contexts.

The two primary matched-document IC50 comparisons favoured FLT4 by 3.60- and 4.54-fold, whereas two additional matched comparisons in the assay-format sensitivity favoured PDGFRA modestly; the corresponding PDGFRA-to-FLT4 IC50 ratios were 0.63 and 0.72 (Fig. 4C). Relaxing only the assay-format annotation recovered three exact, validity-clean, nonduplicate records: PDGFRA IC50=2.3 nM and FLT4 IC50=3.0 and 3.2 nM. Endpoint-specific summaries and document omission retained the pharmacological relevance of both candidates but did not establish a stable receptor-selectivity ordering (Fig. 4D,F). The complete target-level audit comprised 26 raw records: 11 primary records, three additional format-sensitivity records, five duplicate-flagged records, six kinetic records without numeric values and one single-concentration inhibition record (Fig. 4E). The primary maximum pChEMBL values of 8.72 for PDGFRA and 8.30 for FLT4 were preserved; the FLT4 value of 8.52 occurred only in the explicitly labelled expanded sensitivity set. This analysis supports target engagement rather than identifying which receptor causes liver injury or whether its inhibition is protective.

The direct-binding records originate from Davis et al. [73]. Activities 7574898 and 7573179 in CHEMBL1908390 report PDGFRA Kd=16 nM and FLT4 Kd=95 nM, respectively. The accession-linked source document and individual activity records are retained with the analysis.

The exact neutral-parent Z-isomer SMILES for nintedanib was verified against the ChEMBL activity records and the ChEMBL molecule record (CHEMBL502835; InChIKey XZXHXSATPCNXJR-ZIADKAODSA-N). The Inductive Bio connector was used on 2 October 2026 to predict logD at pH 7.4 (mcp_public_logd, version 1.7.0), most acidic pKa and most basic pKa (mcp_public_apka and mcp_public_bpka, version 1.4.0). Exact submitted and returned SMILES, model and configuration versions, raw responses and flags were retained. The connector’s returned lower and upper bounds were reported without assigning an unstated confidence level. These exploratory physicochemical model outputs were not used to modify the target ranking or interpreted as estimates of binding affinity, hepatic safety or molecular dynamics.

Predicted logD at pH 7.4 was 2.523 (returned bounds 1.579–3.447); the most acidic and most basic pKa values were 10.945 (7.998–11.196) and 7.712 (7.409–8.766), respectively. All three connector calls returned successful predictions without out-of-domain or low-confidence flags. These predictions suggest that ligand protonation deserves explicit evaluation when preparing subsequent structural simulations; the connector does not resolve all microscopic protonation states. The bounds have no stated coverage and are not presented as 95% confidence intervals. No binding or MD conclusion was derived from these outputs.

We evaluated donor-balanced networks using a model-conditional intervention analysis, adopting the separation of perturbation effects, no-change controls and context applicability emphasized by State [75]. The analysis did not apply a State checkpoint or predict experimentally validated transcriptional responses. The fixed PDGFRA/FLT4 pair was evaluated in the original hepatocyte, endothelial and macrophage gene universes. Within-donor Ledoit–Wolf correlations, equal-donor averaging, positive top-20 union graphs, the original discovery DO-versus-HV clinical-protein weights and restart probability 0.5 were unchanged. For each target separately and jointly, all incident edges were removed; isolated nodes received self-loops, columns were renormalized, and the original clinical seed vector was propagated again. For each of the 13 clinical genes, the absolute difference between intervened and baseline propagation scores was multiplied by its clinical weight. The sum of these products was divided by the clinical-weighted baseline score to obtain the primary relative magnitude. These scores describe redistribution of network proximity, not changes in transcript abundance or protein release. The exact joint residual was the dual-target score minus each single-target score plus the baseline score; its magnitude used the same weighted absolute metric. KDR and FGFR1 deletions supplied pharmacological comparators. Sham deletion and reapplication of the original graph were numerical controls; restoring the graph was not interpreted as biological rescue.

Background genes excluded all clinical seeds and pharmacological candidates. Each target was matched to its 50 nearest background genes using standardized log1p equal-donor mean expression, logit equal-donor detection with a 0.005 pseudocount, and log1p weighted degree. All 50 single-gene controls and all eligible unique unordered pairs from the two matched pools were evaluated, yielding 1,275 hepatocyte, 1,939 endothelial and 1,275 macrophage pair controls. Upper-tail matched-control probabilities used the plus-one correction. Benjamini–Hochberg correction covered nine target-by-compartment magnitude tests and, separately, three joint-residual tests. All five donor omissions rebuilt the graph within the fixed gene universe; resulting ranges quantify within-atlas sensitivity, not confidence intervals or independent replication. A fixed 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% edge-attenuation series scaled each edge incident to either target once. Target detection was reported by donor, and no sparse context was promoted to an expression-supported result. These settings were specified before their calculation and were not prospectively preregistered. Complete results are retained in Supplementary Figure S11 and the accompanying source-data tables.

Matrix provenance retained GEO accession GSE115469, the deposited normalized measurement convention, original cell identifiers and the five donor labels. The existing data were not pooled with differently quantified counts or relabelled as an independently processed scBaseCount dataset. This provenance design follows the comparability and metadata considerations described by Youngblut et al. [76].

output_text: Single and joint PDGFRA/FLT4 edge deletions generated numerically consistent outputs across donor omissions. The joint deletion changed the clinical-weighted propagation score by 0.000336%, 0.02154% and 0.03848% in hepatocyte, endothelial and macrophage networks, respectively; none of the nine primary effects exceeded matched-control backgrounds after correction (all q≥0.529; Supplementary Fig. S11A–F). Joint residuals also remained nonsignificant after three-test correction (q=0.991, 0.250 and 0.101; Supplementary Fig. S11G,H). Reciprocal receptor-score redistribution was descriptive (Supplementary Fig. S11I). PDGFRA was detected in 8, 33 and 2 cells in the respective compartments, compared with 4, 150 and 13 for FLT4. This analysis defines model-level sensitivity and cellular-coverage requirements and supports the interpretation of PDGFRA and FLT4 as priorities for receptor-specific testing.

output_text: The intervention magnitudes are changes in network scores, not predicted reductions in injury. The results provide no additional evidence for biological synergy, receptor-to-receptor regulation or causal mediation of liver injury.

Reconstruction reproduced all 50 archived primary target–compartment propagation scores, with maximum absolute difference 4.07×10−20. The largest linear-solve residual was 9.71×10−17; sham deletion and graph restoration both returned zero displacement. The latter confirms numerical reversibility of the operator and is not a biological rescue experiment. All full-data, comparator, sham and donor-omission calculations are retained in the 111-row intervention table. The fixed attenuation series scaled shared incident edges once, avoiding double attenuation of the edge between the two targets.

The macrophage joint-residual comparison had nominal P=0.03370 and BH q=0.10110; the corresponding hepatocyte and endothelial q values were 0.99138 and 0.24974. All nine primary magnitude tests had q≥0.52941. Complete target and compartment results are provided in the accompanying tables.

The liver atlas located these quantities within a multicellular tissue. Descriptive embeddings documented hepatocyte, endothelial, and macrophage structure (Supplementary Fig. S12B–D). Equal-donor estimates showed prominent endothelial detection of KDR (31.9%), FLT1 (52.2%), FLT4 (16.2%), and FGFR1 (22.2%). FGFR2 and FGFR3 were most detectable in cholangiocytes; PDGFRA and PDGFRB were most evident in stellate cells, although that compartment comprised only 37 cells from four donors (Supplementary Fig. S12E,G). The injury genes were predominantly hepatocellular: detection reached 94.5% for ALDOB, 84.8% for CES1, 74.2% for CPS1, 58.6% for GSTA1, 54.7% for FBP1, and 29.9% for LECT2 (Supplementary Fig. S12F). This distribution directs the mechanistic question toward non-parenchymal receptor signaling and its effects on hepatocellular injury.

Before evaluating that connection, we audited 95731 gene-level records from 210 virtual-knockout runs (Supplementary Fig. S12H–K). In 132 runs, maximum displacement was at floating-point scale, no greater than 2.85×10−15. The smallest maximum among nonzero runs was 4.73×10−7; classifications were identical using cutoffs of 10−14, 10−12, or 10−10. Of 102 drug-target runs, 73 were numerically zero and 29 were quantifiable. Percentile normalization had assigned ordered scores even to noise-scale distances, so those runs could not support a biological perturbation claim.

FGFR1 illustrated the consequence. Only one of three endothelial runs was numerically nonzero (maximum 6.02×10−6); the other two maxima were approximately 10−15, as was its available macrophage result (Supplementary Fig. S12J). The percentile-normalized scores therefore did not establish reproducible FGFR1 perturbation. Across all 29 quantifiable drug-target runs, projection of the continuous human DILI-versus-non-DILI protein profile did not exceed expression-matched backgrounds (minimum upper-tail P=0.352). The valid FGFR1 endothelial run had standardized difference −2.20 and P=1.000 (Supplementary Fig. S12K). Numerical calibration thus changed the target interpretation and established the need for an independently calibrated way to connect drug pharmacology to the clinical phenotype.

We propagated the continuous protein phenotype through donor-balanced shrinkage networks and evaluated target proximity against matched seed sets (Fig. 5B). The fixed 17-target universe produced 50 evaluable target–compartment combinations; FGFR2 lacked an endothelial value. All primary computations passed numerical checks, with maximum linear-system residual 8.88×10−16 across the 18 graph specifications. Four clinical-weight profiles generated 3600 candidate estimates. Five actual donor omissions generated 250 estimates, including one undefined null-adjusted value retained as unavailable.

Three primary associations reached joint-family q=0.00833: endothelial LRRK2 (Z=27.424), endothelial TYK2 (Z=5.670), and macrophage PDGFRA (Z=7.299). LRRK2 and PDGFRA also met the specified graph- and donor-rank stability requirements. Their same-compartment detection fractions were nevertheless only 4.184% and 0.139%, respectively; TYK2 detection was 5.324%. No candidate satisfied significance, stability, and the specified 10% expression threshold together (Fig. 5C,M). The specified threshold was applied to all candidates.

Seed decomposition explained why apparently large network effects required this qualification. OTC and ALDOB contributed 47.43% and 45.74% of the endothelial LRRK2 score; PCK2 contributed 92.68% for endothelial TYK2, and HPD contributed 91.41% for macrophage PDGFRA (Fig. 5D). The latter receptor was detected in just two cells across two donors. Degree-matched calibration retained the endothelial associations across matching-pool sizes, but macrophage PDGFRA lost FDR significance with the 100-gene pool. Donor omissions also produced negative as well as positive Z values for the endothelial candidates (Fig. 5E). FGFR1 had negative primary null-adjusted scores in all three modeled compartments. These findings identify sparse or concentrated connections, rather than broad, expression-supported disruption of the clinical program.

Changing the clinical contrast or source cohort while retaining the graph gave candidate-rank correlations of 0.838–0.982 with the primary weighting. Unshrunk and shrinkage-conditioned ranks correlated at 0.517 in hepatocytes, 0.821 in endothelial cells, and 0.924 in macrophages, with maximum changes of 13, seven, and five positions. Thus, the human phenotype could be transported across several weighting definitions, but covariance estimation remained consequential, especially in hepatocytes. The comparison identifies covariance estimation as an influential design choice to include in subsequent experimental benchmarking.

The algorithm comparison separated rank stability from predictive evidence. Geometric fusion retained full-data ranks after component omission with mean Spearman correlation 0.833 versus 0.793 for the exact historical consensus, and mean top-five Jaccard overlap 0.607 versus 0.506 (Fig. 5H). Agreement with the omitted feature was weak, however: mean correlation 0.045 for geometric fusion, with maximin highest at 0.115 (Fig. 5I). None of the five integration methods produced a competitive q value below 0.05; minima were 0.139 for robust rank aggregation and 0.178 for geometric fusion. Numerically valid legacy virtual-knockout comparisons were also limited: requiring three evaluable seeds left only two endothelial and two macrophage candidates, insufficient for an informative broad algorithm comparison.

Detailed pulmonary measurements characterized the cellular and protein context of treatment response. In GSE151374, 70696 cells came from 18 pooled libraries; three pools per condition and time supplied the statistical units. Neither macrophage genes, composition, nor prespecified programs showed FDR-controlled treatment effects. The day-14 receptor-tyrosine-kinase program and FGFR1 transcript changes were nominally positive, but each had exact three-versus-three P=0.10 and failed correction (Supplementary Fig. S6). In PXD052594, the unconditioned deposited-animal comparison included 10 nintedanib and 13 vehicle mice after source postrandomization losses. None of 7006 proteins passed q<0.10 (minimum q=0.608), and the prespecified programs were also null (Supplementary Fig. S7). In the separate five-versus-five phosphoproteome subset, an unmoderated parametric screen identified 994 of 20043 sites at q<0.05, with 495 decreases and 499 increases. However, no quantified site in the examined FGFR3, PDGFRA, FLT4, MAPK1, MAPK3, AKT1, or STAT3 tracks passed that threshold, and an FGFR1 site was unavailable. Small-group variance estimation, preprocessing, and unmeasured batch structure limit this table-level sensitivity; absent matched total-protein adjustment also prevents distinguishing phosphorylation changes from protein-abundance shifts. These findings did not provide target-specific functional confirmation.

(A) PDGFRA and FLT4 detection fractions in each of five donors within hepatocyte (Hep; 3,501 cells), endothelial (Endo; 844 cells) and macrophage (Mac; 1,192 cells) compartments. (B) Clinical-weighted absolute propagation-score change for single PDGFRA, single FLT4 and joint (Dual) deletions. Large points show full-atlas values; smaller points show the five donor omissions and horizontal segments their ranges. Ranges are not confidence intervals. (C) BH q values across all nine target-by-compartment magnitude tests. (D) Endothelial relative propagation-score changes for the 13 clinical genes. These are changes in network scores, not gene expression. (E) Endothelial sensitivity to the fixed incident-edge attenuation grid; this is a computational operator series, not a drug concentration–response curve. (F) Full-atlas clinical-weighted changes after PDGFRA, FLT4, KDR and FGFR1 deletions. (G) Clinical-weighted absolute joint residual, fAB−fA−fB+f0, relative to the baseline clinical score, with donor-omission ranges. (H) Matched-control nominal P values and three-test BH q values for the joint residual; no q<0.05. (I) Propagation-score redistribution at the unperturbed receptor after deleting the other receptor; the undirected graph does not establish a regulatory arrow. Matching used expression, detection and degree; each single-target null contained 50 genes, while the unique pair nulls contained 1,275, 1,939 and 1,275 controls in hepatocyte, endothelial and macrophage networks. Sham deletion and graph restoration both returned zero displacement; the largest linear-solve residual was 9.71×10−17. Restoration is an implementation check, not an observed biological rescue.
